html:
The British law of 1833 that ended slavery in most of the British Empire from 1 August 1834. It freed about 800,000 people, most of them in the Caribbean, as well as people in the Cape Colony and Mauritius.

It came after decades of campaigning by abolitionists such as William Wilberforce, after Britain banned the slave trade in 1807, and after a great slave uprising, the Baptist War in Jamaica in 1831 and 1832.

The deal favoured the owners:

  • Slave owners received £20 million in compensation, about 40 per cent of the government's yearly budget. The enslaved got nothing. The loans raised for this were only paid off in 2015.
  • Freed people over the age of six had to keep working for their former owners as unpaid "apprentices". After protests, this ended early, in 1838.
  • Lands run by the East India Company were left out at first.

To replace freed workers, planters soon turned to indentured labourers from India, and slavery at the Cape gave way to new forms of control.
sum: The British law of 1833 that ended slavery in most of the British Empire from 1 August 1834. It freed about 800,000 people, most of them in the Caribbean, as well as people in the Cape Colony and Mauritius.
